title: Advanced Analytical Techniques
source_note: Grounded in standard advanced analytical/instrumental chemistry and laboratory technology content: spectrophotometry, chromatography, electrophoresis, centrifugation, mass spectrometry, ELISA/immunoassay, PCR, and electrochemical methods, as applied to diagnostic and analytical laboratory practice at the 400 level.

questions.question: Beer-Lambert's law relates absorbance to which two variables?
options: Concentration of the analyte and the path length of light through the sample
Wavelength and temperature only
pH and ionic strength
Refractive index and viscosity
questions.correct_answer: Concentration of the analyte and the path length of light through the sample
questions.explanation: Beer-Lambert's law states that absorbance (A) is directly proportional to the molar absorptivity, concentration, and path length (A = εcl).

questions.question: In a spectrophotometer, what is the function of the monochromator?
options: To isolate a specific wavelength of light from a broad light source
To hold the sample cuvette
To detect and amplify the transmitted light
To generate the light source
questions.correct_answer: To isolate a specific wavelength of light from a broad light source
questions.explanation: The monochromator (using a prism or diffraction grating) selects a narrow band of wavelengths for analysis.

questions.question: Why is a blank (reagent blank) used when performing spectrophotometric assays?
options: To zero the instrument and correct for absorbance due to reagents/solvent rather than the analyte
To increase the sensitivity of the assay
To sterilize the cuvette
To calibrate the wavelength selector only
questions.correct_answer: To zero the instrument and correct for absorbance due to reagents/solvent rather than the analyte
questions.explanation: The blank contains all reagents except the analyte, allowing the instrument to be zeroed so that measured absorbance reflects only the analyte of interest.

questions.question: In atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS), what does the technique primarily measure?
options: The absorption of light by free gaseous atoms of an element
The fluorescence emitted by molecules
The mass-to-charge ratio of ions
The rotation of polarized light
questions.correct_answer: The absorption of light by free gaseous atoms of an element
questions.explanation: AAS measures the absorption of specific wavelength light by ground-state free atoms of an element vaporized in a flame or graphite furnace.

questions.question: What is the primary basis of separation in chromatography?
options: Differential partitioning of components between a mobile phase and a stationary phase
Differences in molecular charge only
Differences in magnetic properties
Differences in radioactivity
questions.correct_answer: Differential partitioning of components between a mobile phase and a stationary phase
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates mixture components based on their differing affinities/partitioning between a mobile phase and a stationary phase.

questions.question: In thin layer chromatography (TLC), the Rf value is calculated as:
options: Distance travelled by the solute divided by distance travelled by the solvent front
Distance travelled by the solvent divided by distance travelled by the solute
Total plate length divided by spot diameter
Retention time divided by column length
questions.correct_answer: Distance travelled by the solute divided by distance travelled by the solvent front
questions.explanation: Rf (retention factor) = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent front, used to identify and compare compounds.

questions.question: In gas chromatography (GC), samples must generally be:
options: Volatile and thermally stable
Non-volatile solids only
Radioactive
Highly colored
questions.correct_answer: Volatile and thermally stable
questions.explanation: GC separates volatile compounds carried by an inert gas through a heated column; samples must vaporize without decomposing.

questions.question: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) differs from classical column chromatography mainly by:
options: Using high pressure to force the mobile phase through a densely packed column for faster, higher-resolution separation
Using no stationary phase at all
Only being applicable to gases
Requiring no detector
questions.correct_answer: Using high pressure to force the mobile phase through a densely packed column for faster, higher-resolution separation
questions.explanation: HPLC uses high-pressure pumps to push solvent through a tightly packed column, achieving greater resolution and speed than gravity-fed column chromatography.

questions.question: In ion-exchange chromatography, separation is based primarily on:
options: The electrostatic charge of molecules relative to charged groups on the stationary phase
Molecular size only
Boiling point
Solubility in organic solvents only
questions.correct_answer: The electrostatic charge of molecules relative to charged groups on the stationary phase
questions.explanation: Ion-exchange chromatography separates molecules based on the strength of their ionic interaction with oppositely charged resin groups.

questions.question: Gel filtration (size-exclusion) chromatography separates molecules based on:
options: Molecular size, with larger molecules eluting first
Molecular charge
Hydrophobicity
Affinity for a specific ligand
questions.correct_answer: Molecular size, with larger molecules eluting first
questions.explanation: In gel filtration, larger molecules are excluded from the porous gel beads and elute first, while smaller molecules enter the pores and elute later.

questions.question: What is the principle underlying gel electrophoresis of nucleic acids and proteins?
options: Charged molecules migrate through a gel matrix under an electric field, separating by size and charge
Molecules separate based on boiling point in an electric field
Molecules are separated by centrifugal force
Molecules are separated by magnetic attraction
questions.correct_answer: Charged molecules migrate through a gel matrix under an electric field, separating by size and charge
questions.explanation: In electrophoresis, an electric field drives charged molecules through a gel matrix; smaller molecules migrate faster, achieving separation primarily by size.

questions.question: In agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA, which dye is commonly used to visualize DNA bands under UV light?
options: Ethidium bromide
Crystal violet
Eosin
Methylene blue
questions.correct_answer: Ethidium bromide
questions.explanation: Ethidium bromide intercalates into DNA and fluoresces under UV light, allowing visualization of DNA bands after electrophoresis.

questions.question: In SDS-PAGE (polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis), the role of SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate) is to:
options: Denature proteins and coat them with uniform negative charge so separation depends mainly on size
Stain the proteins for visualization
Provide the electric current
Preserve the native 3D structure of proteins
questions.correct_answer: Denature proteins and coat them with uniform negative charge so separation depends mainly on size
questions.explanation: SDS denatures proteins and binds proportionally to their length, giving them a uniform charge-to-mass ratio so migration through the gel reflects molecular weight.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of centrifugation in laboratory analysis?
options: To separate components of a mixture based on differences in density using centrifugal force
To heat samples for sterilization
To measure the pH of solutions
To amplify DNA fragments
questions.correct_answer: To separate components of a mixture based on differences in density using centrifugal force
questions.explanation: Centrifugation applies centrifugal force to separate particles/components of differing densities, such as separating serum from blood cells.

questions.question: Which type of centrifuge generates extremely high speeds (up to hundreds of thousands of rpm) used to separate subcellular organelles or macromolecules?
options: Ultracentrifuge
Microhematocrit centrifuge
Clinical bench centrifuge
Cytocentrifuge
questions.correct_answer: Ultracentrifuge
questions.explanation: Ultracentrifuges achieve very high speeds and relative centrifugal force sufficient to sediment small particles like ribosomes and viruses.

questions.question: Relative centrifugal force (RCF) in centrifugation depends on which two main factors?
options: Rotor speed (rpm) and radius of rotation
Sample volume and tube material
Ambient temperature and humidity
Sample pH and viscosity only
questions.correct_answer: Rotor speed (rpm) and radius of rotation
questions.explanation: RCF (expressed in x g) is calculated from rotor speed and the radius from the center of rotation to the sample, per the formula RCF = 1.118 x 10^-5 x r x rpm^2.

questions.question: ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) fundamentally relies on which principle?
options: Specific antigen-antibody binding coupled with an enzyme-substrate colorimetric reaction
Separation of molecules by electric charge
Measurement of radioactive decay
Migration of molecules through a gel
questions.correct_answer: Specific antigen-antibody binding coupled with an enzyme-substrate colorimetric reaction
questions.explanation: ELISA detects and quantifies antigens or antibodies using specific immunological binding, with an enzyme-linked reporter producing a measurable colored product.

questions.question: In a sandwich ELISA, the analyte (antigen) is captured between:
options: Two specific antibodies — a capture antibody and a detection (enzyme-linked) antibody
Two identical antigens
A dye and a filter
Two different enzymes with no antibody involved
questions.correct_answer: Two specific antibodies — a capture antibody and a detection (enzyme-linked) antibody
questions.explanation: Sandwich ELISA uses a capture antibody bound to the plate and an enzyme-conjugated detection antibody, sandwiching the target antigen between them.

questions.question: Which enzyme is most commonly conjugated to antibodies in ELISA to produce a colorimetric signal?
options: Horseradish peroxidase (HRP)
DNA polymerase
Amylase
Lysozyme
questions.correct_answer: Horseradish peroxidase (HRP)
questions.explanation: Horseradish peroxidase (along with alkaline phosphatase) is widely used as a reporter enzyme in ELISA to catalyze a color-producing reaction with a substrate.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR)?
options: To exponentially amplify a specific target DNA sequence in vitro
To sequence an entire genome directly
To separate proteins by molecular weight
To measure enzyme kinetics
questions.correct_answer: To exponentially amplify a specific target DNA sequence in vitro
questions.explanation: PCR uses repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension with a thermostable polymerase to exponentially amplify a targeted DNA region.

questions.question: In the PCR cycle, what occurs during the denaturation step?
options: The double-stranded DNA template is heated (typically ~94-95°C) to separate into single strands
Primers bind to complementary DNA sequences
Taq polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands
The reaction mixture is cooled to 4°C for storage
questions.correct_answer: The double-stranded DNA template is heated (typically ~94-95°C) to separate into single strands
questions.explanation: Denaturation heats the reaction to break hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands, producing single-stranded templates for primer annealing.

questions.question: Which enzyme, prized for its thermostability, is commonly used in PCR?
options: Taq polymerase
Pepsin
Trypsin
Catalase
questions.correct_answer: Taq polymerase
questions.explanation: Taq polymerase, derived from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, withstands the high temperatures of PCR denaturation cycles without denaturing.

questions.question: In real-time (quantitative) PCR, fluorescence signal is typically used to:
options: Monitor DNA amplification in real time and quantify the initial amount of target DNA
Denature the DNA template
Stain proteins after separation
Measure pH changes in the reaction
questions.correct_answer: Monitor DNA amplification in real time and quantify the initial amount of target DNA
questions.explanation: qPCR uses fluorescent dyes or probes whose signal increases proportionally with amplicon production, enabling real-time monitoring and quantification.

questions.question: What does mass spectrometry primarily measure?
options: The mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of ionized particles
The color intensity of a solution
The viscosity of a liquid sample
The electrical conductivity of a solution
questions.correct_answer: The mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of ionized particles
questions.explanation: Mass spectrometry ionizes molecules and measures their mass-to-charge ratio, providing information on molecular identity and structure.

questions.question: In mass spectrometry, what is the function of the ion source?
options: To convert sample molecules into gas-phase ions
To separate ions based on charge only
To detect ions after separation
To vaporize the solvent only
questions.correct_answer: To convert sample molecules into gas-phase ions
questions.explanation: The ion source (e.g., electron ionization, electrospray ionization) converts analyte molecules into charged gas-phase ions for subsequent analysis.

questions.question: GC-MS (gas chromatography-mass spectrometry) combines which two capabilities?
options: Separation of volatile compounds with identification/quantification by mass spectrum
Separation of proteins with fluorescent detection
Amplification of DNA with gel visualization
Measurement of pH with conductivity
questions.correct_answer: Separation of volatile compounds with identification/quantification by mass spectrum
questions.explanation: GC-MS couples gas chromatographic separation of volatile compounds with mass spectrometric identification, widely used in toxicology and forensic analysis.

questions.question: In potentiometry, what is measured to determine analyte concentration?
options: The electrical potential (voltage) developed between two electrodes in a solution
The current flowing through a solution
The color change of a redox indicator
The mass of precipitate formed
questions.correct_answer: The electrical potential (voltage) developed between two electrodes in a solution
questions.explanation: Potentiometry measures the electromotive force (potential difference) between a reference and an indicator electrode, related to analyte ion activity (e.g., pH electrodes).

questions.question: A glass pH electrode measures hydrogen ion concentration based on:
options: The potential difference generated across a thin glass membrane selective to H+ ions
Direct titration with a strong acid
Color change of a pH indicator dye
Conductivity of the solution
questions.correct_answer: The potential difference generated across a thin glass membrane selective to H+ ions
questions.explanation: The glass electrode develops a potential proportional to the H+ ion activity difference across its selective glass membrane, calibrated to read pH.

questions.question: Conductometry measures analyte concentration based on:
options: The ability of a solution to conduct electric current, related to ion concentration
The color absorbance of a solution
The refractive index of a solution
The mass-to-charge ratio of ions
questions.correct_answer: The ability of a solution to conduct electric current, related to ion concentration
questions.explanation: Conductometry measures the electrical conductivity of a solution, which depends on the concentration and mobility of ions present.

questions.question: Which technique measures the change in mass of a sample as a function of temperature, used to study thermal stability and decomposition?
options: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)
Nephelometry
Turbidimetry
Fluorometry
questions.correct_answer: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)
questions.explanation: TGA monitors mass changes in a sample as temperature increases, revealing information about decomposition, moisture content, and thermal stability.

questions.question: Nephelometry and turbidimetry both measure light scattering/transmission through a solution, primarily to quantify:
options: Suspended particulate matter or immune complex formation in a sample
The pH of a solution
The temperature of a reaction
The molecular weight of DNA fragments
questions.correct_answer: Suspended particulate matter or immune complex formation in a sample
questions.explanation: Nephelometry (measuring scattered light) and turbidimetry (measuring transmitted light reduction) both quantify particulate matter such as antigen-antibody complexes in solution.

questions.question: What is the main difference between nephelometry and turbidimetry?
options: Nephelometry measures light scattered at an angle; turbidimetry measures the reduction in light transmitted straight through the sample
Nephelometry requires radioactive labels while turbidimetry does not
Turbidimetry can only be used for gases
There is no difference between the two techniques
questions.correct_answer: Nephelometry measures light scattered at an angle; turbidimetry measures the reduction in light transmitted straight through the sample
questions.explanation: Nephelometry detects scattered light at an angle to the incident beam, whereas turbidimetry measures the decrease in the intensity of light transmitted directly through the sample.

questions.question: Fluorometry is based on the principle that certain molecules:
options: Absorb light at one wavelength and emit it at a longer wavelength (fluorescence)
Scatter light equally in all directions regardless of wavelength
Conduct electric current proportional to concentration
Change mass upon heating
questions.correct_answer: Absorb light at one wavelength and emit it at a longer wavelength (fluorescence)
questions.explanation: Fluorometry exploits fluorescent molecules that absorb light at an excitation wavelength and re-emit it at a longer (lower energy) emission wavelength.

questions.question: In quality assurance for analytical methods, what does 'limit of detection (LOD)' refer to?
options: The lowest concentration of an analyte that can be reliably distinguished from background noise
The highest concentration an instrument can measure
The average concentration measured across all samples
The exact concentration required for calibration
questions.correct_answer: The lowest concentration of an analyte that can be reliably distinguished from background noise
questions.explanation: LOD is the smallest analyte concentration that can be detected with reasonable statistical confidence above background/blank noise.

questions.question: Why is calibration with known standards essential before running quantitative analytical assays?
options: To establish a reliable relationship between instrument signal and analyte concentration
To sterilize the instrument
To reduce the cost of reagents
It is not necessary if the instrument is new
questions.correct_answer: To establish a reliable relationship between instrument signal and analyte concentration
questions.explanation: Calibration with standards of known concentration establishes the standard curve/relationship needed to accurately determine unknown sample concentrations.
